title: State of AI: An Empirical 100 Trillion Token Study with OpenRouter
authors: Malika Aubakirova, Alex Atallah, Chris Clark, Justin Summerville, Anjney Midha

findings.claim: Across OpenRouter traffic, average prompt length per request grew from ~1.5K to over 6K tokens, while completions grew from ~150 to ~400 tokens.
findings.quote: Average prompt tokens per request have increased roughly fourfold from around 1.5K to over 6K while completions have nearly tripled from about 150 to 400 tokens.

quantities.condition: late 2025 average; prompts include re-sent conversation history
derived: 6000 / 400

findings.bears_on: Per-request prompts are ~1e5 bits raw, far below K; what matters for K is novel input per session, not per request.

findings.claim: Programming prompts average 3-4 times the length of general-purpose prompts.
findings.quote: programming-related prompts now average 3–4 times the token length of general-purpose prompts

quantities.condition: midpoint of 3-4x

findings.bears_on: Coding and agent workloads set the upper end of honest prompt volume for calibrating K.

title: How Do AI Agents Spend Your Money? Analyzing and Predicting Token Consumption in Agentic Coding Tasks
authors: Longju Bai, Zhemin Huang, Xingyao Wang, Jiao Sun, Rada Mihalcea, Erik Brynjolfsson, et al.

findings.claim: On SWE-bench Verified with OpenHands and eight frontier models, an agentic task uses ~3500x the tokens of a single-round reasoning task and ~1200x a multi-round chat, driven by input tokens.
findings.quote: On average, agentic coding tasks consume 3500x more tokens than a typical single-round reasoning task and 1200x more tokens than a multi-round chatting task.

quantities.condition: SWE-bench Verified, OpenHands, 4 runs x 8 models

findings.bears_on: Agent sessions, not chats, set the inference allowance K must cover.

findings.claim: Per-task token use spans millions: the most expensive instance uses ~7M more tokens than the cheapest.
findings.quote: Across 500 problems, the most expensive instance costs $\sim$ 7M more tokens than the cheapest.

quantities.condition: total billed tokens, mostly cached re-reads

findings.bears_on: Billed tokens per agent task reach ~1e7, i.e. ~1.7e8 bits raw, above K; but most are re-reads (next finding).

findings.claim: Cache reads of previously seen context dominate token volume in every phase; new content enters in spikes (file views, test runs).
findings.quote: We find that cache reads dominate both raw token volume and dollar cost.
findings.bears_on: Re-read context is not novel to a block that holds the session, so novel input per session is far smaller than billed input; K should be calibrated on cache-creation plus uncached tokens.

findings.claim: Agentic coding on SWE-bench-style tasks averages a 153.85:1 input/output token ratio, against 1.33 for code chat and 0.16 for code reasoning.
findings.quote: 0.16 1.33 153.85 Input/Output Ratio

quantities.condition: agentic coding, average over tasks and eight frontier LLMs
derived: 153.85 x (1 - 0.9), combining Bai's ratio with SemiAnalysis's 90% cache hit rate

findings.bears_on: Supports the draft's 153.85:1; the draft's ~15:1 net-new figure mixes this ratio with another source's cache rate, so it is a derived estimate and should be labelled as such.

findings.claim: Cache reads dominate both token volume and cost in every phase of an agentic run.
findings.quote: We find that cache reads dominate both raw token volume and dollar cost. In every phase, cache-read input tokens are the largest category by a wide margin
findings.bears_on: Most input tokens re-read context already seen, so the novel bits per session are far below input tokens times b_tok, which helps inference fit under K.

findings.claim: Agentic coding uses about 3500x more tokens than a single-round reasoning task and 1200x more than multi-round chat.
findings.quote: On average, agentic coding tasks consume 3500x more tokens than a typical single-round reasoning task and 1200x more tokens than a multi-round chatting task
findings.bears_on: Agentic sessions are the inference case most likely to press against K, so NCI's inference allowance should be sized against them.

derived: 1/0.083; lossless

findings.bears_on: b_tok is best defined per byte and converted to per token; the tokenizer changes positions, not entropy.

findings.claim: Chinchilla 70B with arithmetic coding compresses enwik9 (Wikipedia) to 8.3% of its raw size, about 12x, before counting the model's size.

findings.claim: Float16 neural network parameters barely compress losslessly with classical compressors (gzip 92.2%, LZMA2 89.1%).

title: Defeating Nondeterminism in LLM Inference
authors: Horace He

findings.claim: Standard inference servers are not batch-invariant: 1000 greedy runs of Qwen3-235B on one prompt gave 80 distinct completions.

findings.quote: We improve over our no-pruning baseline while training on as little as 30% of the original training dataset.

title: FineZip : Pushing the Limits of Large Language Models for Practical Lossless Text Compression
authors: Fazal Mittu, Yihuan Bu, Akshat Gupta, Ashok Devireddy, Alp Eren Ozdarendeli, Anant Singh, et al.

findings.claim: LLMZip with arithmetic coding on Llama-3-8B compresses 10 MB of enwik8 to 7.95% (0.64 bits per byte) but took about 9.5 days in their implementation.
findings.quote: For LLMZip with AC, the time taken to compress 10MB of data is approximately 9.5 days.
findings.location: Section 3 and Table 1 (LLMZip (AC): 0.0795, 13571 min; bzip2 0.2374; NNCP 0.15021)

quantities.condition: derived: 0.0795 x 8; first 10 MB of enwik8, Llama-3-8B + AC
derived: 0.636 x 3.94 bytes/token

findings.bears_on: Entropy coding against an 8B model works; the cost is sequential decoding (one forward step per token), so throughput, not bits, is the practical limit.

title: Less Impressed, More Involved: A Guide to Using Claude Code Effectively
authors: Rob Moore

findings.claim: One heavy Claude Code user's 30 days: 91.2k uncached input, 792.5k output, 68.8M cache-write and 961.6M cache-read tokens.
findings.location: ccusage table (columns Input, Output, Cache Create, Cache Read, Total Tokens, Cost)

quantities.condition: derived: 961.6M / (68.8M + 0.09M); single user, anecdotal
derived: 68.9M / 0.79M; cache writes include the agent's own earlier outputs

findings.bears_on: New context entering coding sessions is ~1/14 of billed input; ~69M new tokens per month across all sessions bounds novel input per session well below 1e8 bits.
findings.audit: 2026-10-17 sample audit: quote yes, claim yes, quantities derived-ok

title: Learning to Compress Prompts with Gist Tokens
authors: Jesse Mu, Xiang Lisa Li, Noah Goodman

findings.claim: Gisting compresses instruction prompts into a few learned gist tokens, up to 26x, with minimal quality loss on LLaMA-7B and FLAN-T5-XXL.
findings.quote: gisting enables up to 26x compression of prompts, resulting in up to 40% FLOPs reductions, 4.2% wall time speedups, and storage savings, all with minimal loss in output quality.

quantities.condition: LLaMA-7B / FLAN-T5-XXL; instruction prompts, which li-2024-500xcompressor notes are typically under thirty tokens

findings.bears_on: Soft compression shrinks positions, not bits: each gist token is a d-dimensional activation, so it must be charged at activation width, not b_tok.

title: Scaling Data-Constrained Language Models
authors: Niklas Muennighoff, Alexander M. Rush, Boaz Barak, Teven Le Scao, Aleksandra Piktus, Nouamane Tazi et al.

findings.claim: Up to 4 epochs of repeated data cost negligible loss versus unique data; returns from more repetition decay to zero.
findings.quote: We find that with constrained data for a fixed compute budget, training with up to 4 epochs of repeated data yields negligible changes to loss compared to having unique data. However, with more repetition, the value of adding compute eventually decays to zero.

quantities.condition: repetition with negligible loss change, up to 9B parameters and 900B tokens

findings.bears_on: Repetition lets a run reuse committed data: novel data bits per training token fall about 4x at m_A near 1.

title: AI Value Capture - The Shift To Model Labs
authors: Daniel Nishball, Dylan Patel, Cheang Kang Wen, et al.

findings.claim: SemiAnalysis's own Claude Code usage runs at about 300 input tokens per output token, with cache hit rates above 90%.
findings.quote: Agentic workloads have extremely high input-to-output ratios (our Claude Code usage has a ratio of about 300:1) and high cache hit rates (90%+).

quantities.condition: SemiAnalysis internal Claude Code usage
derived: 300 x (1 - 0.9) uncached share

findings.bears_on: Supports the draft's ~300:1 and 90%+ figures; since cached input was already read, net-new input per output token is about 30:1 here, which sets how much prompt a block really reads per output.

title: tiktoken (o200k_base encoding)
authors: OpenAI

findings.claim: GPT-4o, GPT-4.1, o-series and GPT-5 use the o200k_base encoding, whose special tokens sit at ids 199999 and 200018 (about 200k entries).
findings.quote: special_tokens = {ENDOFTEXT: 199999, ENDOFPROMPT: 200018}
findings.location: tiktoken_ext/openai_public.py, o200k_base(); tiktoken/model.py maps "gpt-4o" and "gpt-5" to "o200k_base"

quantities.condition: derived: log2(200019)

findings.bears_on: Upper end of raw b_tok among the frontier tokenizers checked: ~17.6 bits (18 if stored as whole bits).

title: Understanding and counting tokens
authors: OpenAI

findings.claim: OpenAI's rule of thumb for English is about 4 characters, or three-quarters of a word, per token.
findings.quote: 1 token is approximately 4 characters.
findings.location: Use rough estimates for English text

quantities.condition: English, rough estimate

findings.bears_on: Supports the ~4 bytes/token factor for converting bits/byte to b_tok.

title: Byte Latent Transformer: Patches Scale Better Than Tokens
authors: Artidoro Pagnoni, Ram Pasunuru, Pedro Rodriguez, John Nguyen, Benjamin Muller, Margaret Li et al.

findings.claim: The Byte Latent Transformer reaches training-FLOP-controlled parity with Llama 3 up to 8B and 4T bytes.
findings.quote: We show that we achieve training flop -controlled parity with Llama 3 up to 8B scale while having the option to trade minor losses in evaluation metrics for flop efficiency gains of up to 50%

quantities.condition: BLT vs BPE Llama 3, training-FLOP-controlled, up to 8B

findings.bears_on: m_A about 1 at train time; input is raw bytes (8 bits each), so data bits per token-equivalent change.

title: LLMLingua-2: Data Distillation for Efficient and Faithful Task-Agnostic Prompt Compression
authors: Zhuoshi Pan, Qianhui Wu, Huiqiang Jiang, Menglin Xia, Xufang Luo, Jue Zhang, et al.

findings.claim: Task-agnostic extractive compression reaches 2x-5x on MeetingBank, LongBench, ZeroScrolls, GSM8K and BBH.
findings.quote: accelerating the end-to-end latency by 1.6x-2.9x with compression ratios of 2x-5x.

quantities.condition: midpoint of the stated 2x-5x; task-agnostic, faithful (extractive)

findings.bears_on: A conservative central value for lossy task-agnostic prompt compression.

title: The FineWeb Datasets: Decanting the Web for the Finest Text Data at Scale
authors: Guilherme Penedo, Hynek Kydlíček, Loubna Ben allal, Anton Lozhkov, Margaret Mitchell, Colin Raffel et al.

findings.claim: On MMLU, FineWeb-Edu matches the final performance of the Matrix dataset with almost 10x fewer tokens.
findings.quote: On MMLU, FineWeb-Edu can match the final performance of Matrix with almost 10x fewer tokens, demonstrating the effectiveness of classifiers trained on LLM annotations for large-scale data filtering.

quantities.condition: tokens to match Matrix on MMLU, 1.71B ablation models

findings.bears_on: Educational filtering gives a benchmark-specific m_A near 10 at 1.71B; loss-based m_A is smaller.

findings.claim: FineWeb's data ablations train 1.71B-parameter Llama-architecture models.
findings.quote: Data ablation models all had 1.71B parameters (including embeddings), used the Llama architecture
findings.bears_on: Scale of the data-quality multipliers.

title: Pre-training Distillation for Large Language Models: A Design Space Exploration
authors: Hao Peng, Xin Lv, Yushi Bai, Zijun Yao, Jiajie Zhang, Lei Hou et al.

findings.claim: Pre-training distillation of a 1.9B student from GLM-4-9B on 100B tokens improves an average benchmark 1.6%; truncated teacher logits still take about 15 TB.
findings.quote: The truncation reduces storage space by 4, 000× to about 15 TB of disk space. The preliminary PD yields an average performance improvement of 1.6% across a comprehensive set of English and Chinese datasets

quantities.condition: derived: 15 TB of top-p-k logits / 100B tokens

findings.bears_on: 15 TB over 100B tokens is about 1,200 bits of teacher signal per token, about 70x the raw token id.

findings.claim: Larger students gain more from pretraining distillation, and a larger teacher is not necessarily better.
findings.quote: (1) Larger student LLMs generally benefit more from pre-training distillation. (2) Distilling from a larger teacher LLM does not necessarily yield better performance.
findings.bears_on: Downstream metric; consistent with the capacity gap.

findings.claim: Distillation's gain rises early in pretraining, then converges with a slight decrease, still significant at the end.
findings.quote: The gains from pre-training distillation increase initially during pre-training and then converge with a slight decrease, and are still significant are the end of pre-training.
findings.bears_on: The reuse gain decays with the student's own training.

title: Diffusion Beats Autoregressive in Data-Constrained Settings
authors: Mihir Prabhudesai, Mengning Wu, Amir Zadeh, Katerina Fragkiadaki, Deepak Pathak

findings.claim: Diffusion LMs can repeat data for up to 100 epochs with repeated data nearly as good as fresh, versus about 4 for autoregressive models.
findings.quote: In contrast, we find that diffusion models can be trained on repeated data for up to 100 epochs , while having repeated data almost as effective as fresh data

quantities.condition: repetition nearly as effective as fresh data, masked diffusion

findings.bears_on: Diffusion trades compute for data: novel data bits per training token can fall about 100x.

findings.claim: Autoregressive models win at low compute; beyond a critical compute threshold diffusion overtakes them.
findings.quote: autoregressive models initially outperform diffusion models at low compute, but quickly saturate. Beyond a critical compute threshold, diffusion models continue improving and ultimately achieve better performance
findings.bears_on: Diffusion's m_A is below 1 until data is scarce.

title: Haiku to Opus in Just 10 bits: LLMs Unlock Large Compression Gains
authors: Roy Rinberg, Annabelle Michael Carrell, Simon Henniger, Nicholas Carlini, Keri Warr

findings.claim: The paper discusses egress limiting, capping the bits that leave a datacenter, as a defense for model weights.
findings.quote: One promising defense for protecting model weights is egress limiting: restricting the total number of bits that exit a datacenter
findings.bears_on: Supports the draft's citation for egress limits; it is a governance analogue of NCI's per-block read bound K.

findings.claim: Domain-adapted LoRAs make LLM arithmetic coding of LLM-generated text lossless at a ratio of 0.09 versus 0.18 for the base model, a 2x gain (about 11x overall, not 33x).
findings.quote: the correct LoRA achieves a compression ratio of 0.09, a 2.0× improvement over the base model (0.18)

quantities.condition: derived: 1/0.09; lossless, relative to log2(vocab) bits per token, Mistral-7B-Instruct with the matching domain LoRA
derived: base model ratio 0.18 x 14.97

findings.bears_on: DISCREPANCY: the LoRA plus arithmetic-coding result is lossless at about 11x, not 33x; it sets entropy-coded b_tok near 1.3-2.7 bits per token for LLM-generated text, versus 17-20 raw.

findings.claim: The roughly 0.03 ratio (about 33x) comes from a lossy method, prompting a model for a succinct rewrite and then arithmetic-coding it, not from the domain-adapted LoRAs.
findings.quote: prompting a model for a succinct rewrite then applying arithmetic coding can achieve compression ratios of approximately 0.03
findings.location: abstract; Section 4.1 (response rewriting; AIME summarization with Opus 0.039 at N=1 to 0.034 at N=10)

quantities.condition: derived: 1/0.03; lossy succinct rewrite plus arithmetic coding, Claude models on AIME responses
derived: 0.03 x about 16.6 bits per raw token (log2 of a ~100k vocabulary)

findings.bears_on: DISCREPANCY: the draft attributes 33x to 'domain-adapted LoRAs and LLM-based arithmetic coding', but 33x is the lossy rewrite method and the ratio is against log2(vocab) bits per token, not bytes; lossy b_tok can be about 0.5 bits per original token.

findings.claim: Ten binary questions from a small model to a large one recover 23-72% of the capability gap on standard benchmarks, at ratios of 0.0006 to 0.004 (about 250-1667x).
findings.quote: 10 binary questions recover 23% to 72% of the capability gap between a small and large model on standard benchmarks and 7% to 38% on harder benchmarks, achieving compression ratios of 0.0006 to 0.004
findings.location: abstract; Section 3 and Table 1 (ratio uses about 16.61 bits per token, cl100k_base; footnote on GPQA)

quantities.condition: recovers 23-72% of the Haiku-to-Opus gap on standard benchmarks, 7-38% on harder ones
derived: 1/0.0006, best case; 1/0.004 = 250x worst case

findings.bears_on: DISCREPANCY: 250-1667x is not lossy compression of the response; it buys only part of the capability gap (and for multiple-choice GPQA the paper's footnote calls it 'technically an expansion'), so it bounds capability.bits rather than b_tok.

title: Tokenomics: Quantifying Where Tokens Are Used in Agentic Software Engineering
authors: Mohamad Salim, Jasmine Latendresse, SayedHassan Khatoonabadi, Emad Shihab

findings.claim: In ChatDev multi-agent runs on GPT-5, tokens per task split 53.9% input, 24.4% output, 21.6% reasoning: about 2:1 input to output.
findings.quote: On average, the overall token usage for each task analyzed is composed of $53.9\%$ input tokens, $24.4\%$ output tokens, and $21.6\%$ reasoning tokens.

quantities.condition: derived: 53.9 / 24.4; 30 ChatDev tasks, GPT-5

findings.bears_on: Multi-agent pipelines are far less input-dominated than single-agent coding; the input:output ratio is workload-specific.

title: Prediction and Entropy of Printed English
authors: Claude E. Shannon

findings.claim: Human prediction experiments put the entropy of literary English at about one bit per letter with long-range context.
findings.quote: in ordinary literary English, the long range statistical effects (up to 100 letters) reduce the entropy to something of the order of one bit per letter, with a corresponding redundancy of roughly 75%.

quantities.condition: human predictors, context up to 100 letters; bounds roughly 0.6-1.3

findings.bears_on: Classic baseline: modern LLMs (~0.53 bpc) already beat Shannon's human-prediction estimate, so ~2 bits/token is plausible for English.

title: Scaling Retrieval-Based Language Models with a Trillion-Token Datastore
authors: Rulin Shao, Jacqueline He, Akari Asai, Weijia Shi, Tim Dettmers, Sewon Min et al.

findings.claim: Larger datastores improve retrieval LMs at the same training compute, without obvious saturation up to 1.4T tokens.
findings.quote: By plotting compute-optimal scaling curves with varied datastore, model, and pretraining data sizes, we show that using larger datastores can significantly improve model performance for the same training compute budget.
findings.bears_on: Datastore size is a compute-free axis of m_A for knowledge tasks.

title: D4: Improving LLM Pretraining via Document De-Duplication and Diversification
authors: Kushal Tirumala, Daniel Simig, Armen Aghajanyan, Ari S. Morcos

quantities.condition: D4 vs deduplicated baseline, 6.7B

findings.bears_on: m_A about 1.2 at 6.7B.

authors: Chandra Shekhara Kaushik Valmeekam, Krishna Narayanan, Dileep Kalathil, Jean-Francois Chamberland, Srinivas Shakkottai

findings.claim: LLaMA-7B plus arithmetic coding reaches 0.71 bits per character on text8 with 511 tokens of memory, about 3.2 bits per token (4.57 chars per token).
findings.quote: When LLaMA-7B is combined with an Arithmetic coder for compression, we obtain a compression ratio of 0.7101 bits/character on a 1MB section of the text8 dataset
findings.location: Section I and Table II (N_c = 4,568,855 chars for N_t = 1,000,000 tokens, M = 511)

quantities.condition: derived: 0.7101 bpc x 4.569 chars/token; text8 (lowercase, no punctuation), LLaMA-7B, 32k vocab
derived: log2(32000), the LLaMA SentencePiece vocabulary stated in Section IV

findings.bears_on: Even a 2023 7B model cuts b_tok to ~3 bits/token; this is an upper anchor for entropy-coded b_tok.

findings.claim: Compression improves with context: 0.91 bpc at 31 tokens of memory versus 0.71 bpc at 511.
findings.quote: As expected, the compression performance improves with increasing $M$.
findings.location: Section IV and Table II (M = 31: 0.9145 bpc; M = 511: 0.7101 bpc)

quantities.condition: derived: 0.9145 bpc x 4.569 chars/token at M = 31

findings.bears_on: Long agent contexts should push b_tok lower than short-window benchmarks suggest; short prompts compress worse.
findings.audit: 2026-10-17 sample audit: quote yes, claim yes, quantities derived-ok

findings.claim: On a book released after the model's training (less contamination), the rate rises to 0.84 bpc.

quantities.condition: 100 KB of a May 2023 Project Gutenberg book, LLaMA-7B + AC

findings.bears_on: Novel (unseen) text costs ~20% more bits than possibly-memorized Wikipedia; b_tok estimates on public benchmarks are optimistic.

title: Beyond Random Sampling: Efficient Language Model Pretraining via Curriculum Learning
authors: Yang Zhang, Amr Mohamed, Hadi Abdine, Guokan Shang, Michalis Vazirgiannis

findings.claim: Curriculum ordering cuts steps to baseline performance by 18-45% in early and mid training.

title: An Empirical Study on Prompt Compression for Large Language Models
authors: Zheng Zhang, Jinyi Li, Yihuai Lan, Xiang Wang, Hao Wang
venue: ICLR 2025 Workshop on Building Trust in LLMs; arXiv preprint

findings.claim: On LongBench, moderate prompt compression can improve performance, while for short contexts every method degrades as compression increases.
findings.quote: All methods' performance decreases with increasing compression ratios for short contexts, but for long contexts, moderate compression can improve performance.
findings.location: Section 1 (findings); abstract: 'In the Longbench evaluation, moderate compression even enhances LLM performance.'

quantities.condition: derived: default rho = 1 - Lc/Lo = 0.5 gives 1/(1-0.5) = 2x; GPT-3.5-turbo, GPT-4o-mini, Claude-3-Haiku

findings.bears_on: DISCREPANCY: this is an empirical study, not a survey, and the gains are at moderate compression (default rho = 0.5, about 2x), not 10x; the 10x-with-gains claim belongs to jha-2024-promptcompression.

findings.claim: The study defines its ratio as the fraction of tokens removed and uses 0.5 by default.
findings.quote: We set it to 0.5
findings.location: Section 4.3 (Implementations); ratio defined as rho = 1 - Lc/Lo
findings.bears_on: Readers converting to NCI's b_tok must use 1/(1-rho), so rho = 0.9 is 10x and the default is 2x.
